abstract
INTRODUCTION: Stiff person syndrome is a rare autoimmune, neurological disorder characterized by progressive
rigidity and episodic painful spasms, predominantly affecting the proximal limbs and axial muscles, and leading to
progressive disability. We report the case of a child who developed symptoms compatible with stiff person
syndrome during treatment for pleuropulmonary blastoma.
PATIENT DESCRIPTION: A 3-year, 5-month-old girl was
admitted for gradually worsening postural tremor, painful spasms, and generalized stiffness. Since the age of 3
years, she had been on adjuvant chemotherapy for pleuropulmonary blastoma before surgical resection. Brain
magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalographic ﬁndings were normal. Although serologic tests for
autoimmune disease, including paraneoplastic antibodies and antiglutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies, were
unremarkable, her ﬁndings were attributed to a paraneoplastic syndrome based on her clinical features and
medical history. However, following the planned pulmonary lobectomy, her symptoms were paradoxically
aggravated, with continuous motor unit potential at rest on electromyography, which occurs in stiff person syn-
drome. She gradually improved during postadjuvant chemotherapy with simultaneous immunotherapy including
intravenous immunoglobulins and methylprednisolone, and she had recovered completely when evaluated at the
22-month follow-up visit after completion of her treatment for pleuropulmonary blastoma.
CONCLUSION: We
present the ﬁrst documented child with stiff person syndrome associated with pleuropulmonary blastoma. The
marked clinical improvement following chemotherapy for pleuropulmonary blastoma was yet more proof of the
pleuropulmonary blastoma-related stiff person syndrome. In children with a malignancy and stiff person syn-
drome, a paraneoplastic syndrome should be considered and the treatment for the malignancy must be
undertaken.

Patient Description
This 3-year, 5-month-old girl was admitted for gradually worsening
postural tremor, painful spasms of both the hands and lower extremities,
and generalized stiffness that had developed 2 months previously. At age
3 years, she had been diagnosed with pleuropulmonary blastoma in her
left hemithorax and then began adjuvant chemotherapy
for pleuropulmonary blastoma for one month before undergoing surgi-
cal resection. A huge lung mass was seen on a chest computed tomog-
raphy scan that was performed to evaluate prolonged fever just before
the diagnosis of pleuropulmonary blastoma ( Fig 1 A). Her birth and
developmental history and her family ’s medical history were
unremarkable.
Her symptoms began as tightness in the upper limbs and deterio-
rated into muscle stiffness of the trunk that was reduced during sleep.
She also suffered from bilateral arm tremors and uncontrolled falls
without loss of consciousness. There was no diurnal ﬂuctuation in these
falling attacks. Physical examination showed truncal stiffness and ri-
gidity of both the arms and the legs that was more severe in the right arm
than in the left. Because of severe leg stiffness, she was completely un-
able to walk. However, cranial nerve examination, the cerebellar function
test, and deep tendon re ﬂexes at all sites were normal.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography,
performed to evaluate for seizures, were unremarkable. Serologic tests
for autoimmune disease, including anti-GAD antibodies and paraneo-
plastic or other autoimmune disease-related antibodies, such as anti-Hu,
anti-Yo, anti-Ri, anti-Tg, anti-thyroid peroxidase, thyroid-stimulating
hormone receptor, and neuromyelitis optica antibody, were unremark-
able. Serologic test for antiamphiphysin antibody or antiglycin receptor
antibody was not done. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid did not contain autoimmune
antibodies, including anti-GAD antibodies. Despite the absence of sero-
logic abnormalities, her tremor and spasticity were attributed to a par-
aneoplastic syndrome based on her clinical features and medical history.
Therefore, pleuropulmonary blastoma treatment was continued with
medication including dantrolene, baclofen, and diazepam to control her
symptoms.
According to the therapeutic plan for pleuropulmonary blastoma,
she underwent pulmonary lobectomy two months following the onset of
her neurological symptoms. However, after her lobectomy, her symp-
toms were paradoxically aggravated and she experienced generalized
stiffness with swallowing dif ﬁculties and dysarthria. At that time, she

could not sit or change her position by herself and could only control her
facial muscles and ﬁngertips. The electromyography showed prominent,
continuous motor unit potential at rest in the right gastrocnemius, right
tibialis anterior, left trapezius, and left biceps brachii, ﬁndings typical of
stiff person syndrome ( Fig 2 ). With her diagnosis of paraneoplastic stiff
person syndrome, we continued her chemotherapy for pleuropulmonary
blastoma with simultaneous immunotherapy including intravenous
immunoglobulins (400 mg/kg for 5 days) and methylprednisolone
(30 mg/kg for 4 days). She gradually improved during the postadjuvant
chemotherapy. Her symptoms gradually resolved, her spasms and falling
attacks disappeared, and she could ﬁnally sit and move her upper limbs
by herself.
At age 4 years and 3 months, after completing chemotherapy, she
tapered her antispasmodic medications and no rigidity or spasms
remained. At her 22-month follow-up examination after completion of
her pleuropulmonary blastoma treatment, she had recovered completely
without any motor or cognitive de ﬁcits.
